title: Consistent hashing on a ring
idea: Consistent hashing places servers and keys on one circle of hash values. Each key belongs to the next server clockwise, so a resize moves only nearby keys.
points: Servers and keys hash into one range; the largest value wraps to zero.
A key belongs to the first server at or after its position, going clockwise.
Adding or losing a server moves only the keys in its slice.
A server can own many ring points, called virtual nodes, which evens out load.

hero.title: Servers join and leave the ring

steps.caption: Servers and keys hash onto the same ring. Each key belongs to the first server clockwise from it.
Add server D. Only the keys between B and D change owner. Every other key stays put.
Server B fails. Its keys move to the next server clockwise, D. No other key moves.
Add E with three points on the ring, called virtual nodes. It takes small slices from several servers.

code.title: A ring with virtual nodes
code.caption: Compare load with one point and with 200, then the keys moved by a ring and by `hash % N`.

walk.text: A well-spread hash and 1000 sample keys. SHA-1 is used for its spread, not for security.
Each server gets `vnodes` points on the ring, sorted by position. Each point is a virtual node.
A key goes to the first point at or after its hash, wrapping past the end.
Count how many keys each server owns.
One point per server is lopsided; many points even it out.
Add server D and count the keys that change owner.
The same change under `hash % N` moves far more keys.

pitfalls: Too few ring points per server gives uneven load; use many virtual nodes.
Moving keys is still work: copy data or refill caches when the ring changes.
All clients need the same server list and hash function, or keys scatter.

quiz.why: A key goes to the first point at or after its hash. 40 sits exactly on B, and 95 wraps around to A.

takeaway: A ring turns a resize from a mass remap into a small, local move.
